ops.markdown:
Paste all three briefs into the same box and treat them as one prompt.

They look like one problem because they share a shape — someone needs words written, and a model writes words. They are three products with three failure modes, and each costs money in a different way.

Classify by **what is hard about it**. Not by what it produces, not by who asked, not by how urgent it is. The tool follows the diagnosis.

---

**On the name.** "Structure / substance / style" comes from the recording's own section bookmark. The instructor never calls it a framework and the class notes carry no trace of this section. The idea is the lecture's spine; the label is not written down anywhere.

ops.title: None of them checks its own facts

ops.markdown:
> All three produce finished-looking content. **None of them checks its own facts.**

It is not that they are inaccurate. The polish and the accuracy are produced by different processes, and only one of them is running. Everything comes back looking like a finished draft, because looking finished is what these tools are for. Whether the numbers in it are the numbers you supplied is a question nobody in the loop has asked.

**The skill has two halves, equally weighted.** Match the tool to the job. Then read every draft before it ships.

So the time does not work the way it first appears. You are not saving the writing time and keeping the reviewing time. You trade a long writing pass for a short generation plus a real review pass. The review is not overhead — it is the part of the job that stayed yours.

---

**Read the *what you supply* column.** Gamma wants a brief, a description of what you want made. Claude and ChatGPT want the raw material itself, unformatted. Canva wants examples of your previous output — neither a description nor raw material, but a demonstration of a target. Three different input shapes, which is the real reason the tools are not interchangeable. Hand Gamma your messy notes and it treats them as a brief and builds a deck around them.

ops.title: How a rate limit actually bites

ops.markdown:
Whatever you are doing, there is a certain number of times it will let you do it. After that it stops you and gives you a cool-off period.

Worked on the board with a limit of **1,000 tokens per five minutes**:

| | Prompt | Response | Running total |
|---|---|---|---|
| Question 1 | 100 | 300 | 400 |
| Question 2 | 500 | 200 | **1,100 — limit hit** |

**The detail worth noticing is which part gets cut off.** It is the second *response*, not the second prompt. The window's budget was already spent by the time the model was writing, so you get a truncated answer rather than a refusal at the door.

In practice: the "you have reached your limit, try again in a few hours" message on Claude, or ChatGPT declining a fourth edit to an image you keep tweaking.

---

**One thing the notes get ambiguous.** Their rate-limiting annotation has an arrow that could point at one column or several. The recording settles it — rate limiting covers Claude, ChatGPT *and* Canva. Gamma is the odd one out, rationed by credits instead.

Canva's exact limits were asked about in class and never answered. They stay unknown rather than guessed.

ops.label: The brief
ops.detail:
Not a one-liner. Farah's carried the meeting context, a seven-slide spec, who the company is, last season's numbers, the proposed deal terms, the trial window, and a style instruction: bold and confident rather than corporate, visual rather than text-heavy.

Entry routes: generate from a prompt, paste in text, use a template, or import a file or URL. Gamma now drops even the generate route into the create-with-agent page; the older flow gave more up-front control over tone and look.

ops.label: Outline — content cards, not slides
ops.detail: The one review gate before anything is rendered. The middle pane shows what each slide will contain, not what it will look like. You can merge slides, add slides, or ask the agent to insert one at this stage.

ops.label: Settings — theme, visuals, image source
ops.detail: Themes chosen for the balance of text and layout. Image source set to stock photos: already shot and licensed for reuse. The free tier pulls from the free pool.

ops.label: Generate — under a minute
ops.detail: Seven slides, images placed, text written. The instructor flagged "under a minute" as load-bearing before the demo started, and came back to it as the explanation for the hallucination.

ops.label: Edit through the agent
ops.detail: The right-hand pane is an AI assistant. Paste a slide's text in, ask for a change, and it inserts in the right place and offers an original-versus-modified diff.

ops.label: A deck you still have to proofread

ops.markdown:
Asked to add a slide on what happens if the guaranteed room-night minimum is not met, Gamma produced one saying the company **will adjust its commission to reflect the shortfall**, **can extend the trial period**, and **is open to renegotiating terms**.

None of it was in the brief. Three commercial concessions, invented, on a slide destined for a partner negotiation. Not three adjectives — three things the presenter would have been standing in the room defending.

**The quieter one is worse.** A pre-class run of the same prompt turned a *four-person core team* into *four full-time founders*. That is not invention from nothing. It is a supplied fact quietly upgraded into a different claim, and it survives a skim by someone who knows the brief.

---

## Why it happens

**It fills gaps rather than flagging them.** Gamma understands its job as producing the presentation. Incomplete information is a hole in a slide, and holes in slides are the thing it exists to prevent.

**Creative choices mean a higher temperature.** Which layout, which image, how the text should read. Higher temperature raises the probability of hallucination.

So speed and invention are not two properties you trade off against each other. **They are the same setting.** That is why Gamma sits at the organising-it end: it does organise your output, at the cost of not being accurate every single time.

A better system prompt helps only to a degree. You can steer it toward your supplied documents, but if the content is not clean you still get a deck, and you still proofread the whole thing before it leaves your hands.

The honest accounting, in answer to a student asking what the point is if it is fast but wrong:

> Something that would have taken four to five hours now takes about half an hour to proofread and get it out.

And explicitly: this does not take away the analyst's job. It makes the task faster so their expertise in their actual field gets used on something better.

**Where it fits outside travel:** pitching an architecture or a solution you have not built yet; proposing a project to leadership.

It is a documenting-and-sharing tool, not an automation tool.

ops.title: The constraint did the work, not the model

ops.markdown:
The prompt's constraints mattered more than any of its writing instructions:

> Use only facts. Do not round, revert or re-tier any number. The notes correct themselves in one place — read carefully and follow the correction. **If anything is ambiguous or missing, do not guess — list it at the end under *Open questions*.**

Because guessing was forbidden, Claude appended an open-questions section rather than inventing answers to the ambiguous parts.

---

**Set this beside Gamma.** Same category of gap in the input. Gamma filled it silently with three commercial concessions. Claude surfaced it as a list of questions.

The difference is not that one model is more honest. **One was told what to do with a gap and the other was not.** The instruction is what converted a hallucination into a visible question. That is the transferable move from this whole section.

**The open-questions section is correct behaviour, and it is internal.** Strip it before the document reaches its readers. Two fixes ran in the same chat: removing that section, and a rupee symbol rendering as an empty box — a font glyph problem, solved by switching to a font that carries the glyph.

ops.markdown:
Within a chat session the artifact stays **a single object**. Revisions edit that same artifact rather than spawning a new file, so nobody ends up holding a stale download — whenever they open it, they get the current version.

This is the practical reason to prefer this path for anything that will be revised. You can create a PDF in a deck tool, but it would not be as accurate or as easy to change.

**The HTML carried its CSS inline**, in the same file. One self-contained thing that opens directly in a browser and can be handed over as a plain file. A content delivery network is the grown-up way to serve a page; a single self-contained file is the simpler one.

**Publishing.** The publish control is unavailable in an incognito chat — that was diagnosed live in class when it appeared greyed out. Outside incognito it produces a shareable URL on the free tier.

**The published link expires.** Confident it lasts at least a couple of weeks; the actual expiry was not known and is not recorded here as a figure.

ops.label: The input is raw material, not a brief
ops.detail: Phone-typed notes where every fact is real and present, but nothing is clean. Hand this to a deck tool and it reads the whole pile as a brief.

ops.label: It corrects itself mid-sentence
ops.detail: The notes name one starting city, then immediately say no, it changed, use the other one now. The tool has to follow the correction rather than average the two. A tool that treats input as a brief will happily produce a document mentioning both.

ops.label: Non-standard shorthand
ops.detail: Per person as PP, people as PPL, and the general register of typing fast on a phone. These are non-standard to a company but common enough worldwide to be well represented in training data.

ops.label: At least one ambiguous number
ops.detail: The notes refer to the cancellation policy by a shorthand that only reads as a slab boundary if you already know the policy. This is exactly the kind of gap the do-not-guess constraint is written for.

ops.title: Canva Magic Studio — the LinkedIn pipeline

ops.label: Past posts in as voice examples
ops.detail: The examples are the input that matters. Drawn from the channel you are writing for, not from the brand as a whole.

ops.label: Magic Write generates the batch
ops.detail: Built for volume — many pieces at once, matched to the examples rather than to a written instruction.

ops.label: Proofread — its own pass
ops.detail: Separate from generation, and not optional. Matching the voice is not the same as being correct: the third tool in the lecture that produces finished-looking content without checking its own facts.

ops.title: Voice is per channel, not per brand

ops.markdown:
The tool learns a voice from examples you give it. That makes the question **which examples**, and the answer is not "ours".

> The LinkedIn voice is not the Instagram voice.

So the example set is assembled per channel. "Our voice" is not one asset you train once and reuse — it is a set of them, one per place you publish, and feeding the wrong set produces copy that is fluent, on-brand in the abstract, and wrong for where it is going.

The practical consequence is that the work is in curating the examples, not in writing the prompt. A style guide describing the voice does less than a handful of posts that are already in it.

ops.value: Your past posts from that channel — examples, not a style guide
